opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of young researchers look at what's happening right now, these huge models, the enormous compute budgets, the big labs, and they feel like everything important is already being done by someone else, or that the field is moving so fast they'll never catch up. I understand that feeling. But I don't think it matches how progress actually happens.

If you look back over the history of AI, and computer vision and graphics in particular, every few years people thought the main problems were nearly solved. Then a new question came up that nobody had good tools for. When I started working on generative models, GANs were barely working. The images were tiny and blurry, and many people thought it was a toy. A few years later we were generating photorealistic faces and turning sketches into landscapes. Now we're talking about world models, physical AI, and systems that can simulate and reason about the 3D world. Each wave created more open problems than it closed.

So my first point is that the frontier keeps expanding. We are nowhere near the end. Physical AI, robotics, embodied intelligence, making models understand physics and causality, making them efficient and reliable: these are wide open. There is plenty of room for new people with fresh ideas.

Second, being nervous doesn't help you do good research. Research needs curiosity and patience. If you're anxious all the time about whether you're working on the "right" trendy topic, you end up chasing what everyone else is doing, and that's the most crowded place to be. The best work I've seen usually came from people who picked a problem they genuinely cared about and stayed with it long enough to understand it deeply.

Third, the fundamentals don't go out of date. Math, optimization, understanding data, thinking clearly about a problem, writing good code, running careful experiments. Models will change and architectures will change, but people with strong foundations can adapt to whatever comes next. Tools like AI coding assistants actually make individual researchers more powerful than before. One person can now do what used to take a small team.

So my advice is to stay calm, stay curious, and build real skills. Pick problems that excite you, not just the ones that are hot this month. The field needs people who think differently, and that's exactly what young researchers bring.

r001.rationale: The response says that seeing huge models, large compute budgets, and big labs can make young researchers feel that everything important is already being done by others, conveying a perception of shrinking research opportunities.

fable-5.1.text:
I tell them not to be nervous because the thing they're worried about—that AI will make their skills obsolete—actually misunderstands what this moment is. We are at the very beginning of something, not the end.

When I was a graduate student, the big question was whether neural networks would even work. The field was small. Nobody at a party wanted to hear about it. Now, every few months there is a result that would have seemed impossible a year earlier, and people look at that and feel the ground moving under them. They think: by the time I finish my PhD, whatever I'm studying will be solved by a bigger model.

But look at what actually happens when a capability becomes cheap. When image classification got good, it didn't eliminate vision research. It opened up generation, 3D, video, world models, simulation—whole areas that were not even possible to work on before, because the foundation wasn't there. Every time the frontier moves, the number of interesting problems grows, it doesn't shrink. The tools get better, and so the ambition of what you can attempt gets bigger.

The other thing I tell them is that the fundamentals don't change as fast as the headlines. Understanding optimization, understanding data, understanding how to design an experiment and know whether you're fooling yourself—that is durable. A person with good taste in problems, who can look at a messy result and figure out what's really going on, that person is valuable in any version of the future. The models are tools. Someone still has to decide what to build with them, and that judgment is exactly what a research training gives you.

And honestly, if you're going to be anxious, the right thing to be anxious about is not whether there will be work. It's whether you're working on something you actually care about. Because there is so much opportunity right now that the main risk is spending your time on something that bores you. Pick a hard problem that matters to you, build real things, and the future will take care of itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes young researchers seeing rapid AI results in the headlines and fearing that their research will be solved by the time they finish their PhD, capturing the perception that opportunities are narrowing.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s natural to feel nervous, because AI is moving so quickly. As a young researcher, you might wonder whether the problem you’re working on will still matter in a year, or whether you can contribute when so many people are working in the field. But rapid progress also creates new questions. There’s still a lot we don’t understand and a lot we don’t know how to do well.

My advice is to focus on what you can control: build strong fundamentals, stay curious, and learn to identify important problems. A particular technique may become outdated, but the ability to ask good questions and test your ideas remains valuable. You don’t need to predict the entire future of AI to make a meaningful contribution to it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions worries about whether one can contribute amid rapid progress and many researchers, but it does not connect those worries to AI publicity or say that publicity makes research opportunities seem narrower.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the uncertainty can actually be exciting. If you’re a young researcher, you don’t need to predict exactly where AI will be in five or ten years. You need to develop the ability to ask good questions, learn new things, and test your ideas carefully. Those skills will remain useful even as the tools change.

Of course, there are real concerns about how AI will affect people. But being nervous by itself doesn’t help us address them. Working on problems you care about does. There’s still so much we don’t understand, and that means there’s room for you to contribute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty, changing tools, and room to contribute, but it does not warn that AI publicity can make young researchers perceive their research opportunities as increasingly narrow.
